A1.justification: Both PDFs describe USMoE by the same authors, with directly matchable methods and experiments despite the changed title. All 18 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original MTEB evaluations, Transformer-XL pretraining and classification fine-tuning results, and routing ablations and analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports original language experiments and adds Alpaca fine-tuning, image classification, corruption and adversarial evaluations, and scoring-function analyses.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 replaces the Expert Choice component's sequence-axis softmax in v1 with elementwise sigmoid in v2. This substantively changes a central routing score and its dependence on other tokens. The weighted combination with Token Choice scores and flattened top-pair selection remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds Alpaca instruction fine-tuning and image classification on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, STL-10, SVHN, and ImageNet-1K. It also adds corrupted language inputs and adversarial vision scenarios. The earlier MTEB, four pretraining corpora, and four downstream classification datasets remain covered.

E2.justification: SoftMoE becomes an evaluated comparator in the new clean and attacked vision comparisons, Tables 3–4. The earlier MTEB comparators Router, TC, EC, and MoEE remain, as do SMoE, SMoE-DR, XMoE, and StableMoE in the retained pretraining and classification comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include GaLore full-parameter Alpaca fine-tuning for 2,000 steps with evaluation every 10 steps, 10M/110M ViT-MoE evaluations, AAA-token text corruption, and PGD, FGSM, and SPSA attacks. These extend the experimental design substantially; the documented protocols for retained MTEB and Transformer-XL experiments remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds sigmoid-versus-softmax analyses of BPC, token dropping, and prompted versus unprompted embeddings, plus language corruption tests, vision attack tests, and visual routing case studies. The earlier sequence-versus-batch and mixing-weight ablations are retained in Tables 10–11, and the earlier router analyses remain in Figures 9–12.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies three runs with different random seeds and reports mean and standard deviation for the vision results in Table 3. The earlier ten-run MTEB reporting remains in Figure 8, formerly Figure 3; no increase in runs for those existing experiments is established.

E6.justification: MTEB USMoE scores are extensively revised alongside the scoring change: the unprompted OLMoE average changes from 39.2 to 45.3, while prompted Qwen summarization changes from 48.4 to 31.0. v2 also adds Alpaca learning curves, corrupted pretraining results, and clean and attacked vision scores. The earlier pretraining and classification results remain in Tables 12–14.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a binary routing optimization with a global assignment budget, Proposition 3.1 asserting optimality against any feasible routing matrix, a general routing definition, and an additional optimality proof in A.3.3. The earlier score-ordering and Jacobian arguments are largely retained in A.3.1–A.3.2 rather than replaced.

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from a competitive-learning interpretation to routing optimization through linear programming under fixed computational budgets. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the claimed effectiveness to vision and corrupted/adversarial conditions, while the introduction adds information-leakage handling. The headline 10% performance and 14% inference-cost claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 newly attributes leakage to softmax and batch-wise selection, interprets sigmoid as capturing semantics and softmax as exploiting in-context cues, and interprets corruption results as evidence of superior robustness and generalization. It also discusses suitability for edge devices. The earlier computational-scale limitations and ethics statements are retained at the appendix's end.

D1.justification: v2 supplies implementation information for the new SFT experiments, including GaLore, the training duration, and evaluation frequency, plus vision model sizes and named corruption procedures. Existing quantization, hardware, batch sizes, optimizer schedules, and implementation links remain. Detailed vision training configurations and attack strengths are not supplied.

R1.justification: The competitive-learning discussion and its comparison with CompeteSMoE are replaced by linear/integer programming positioning in Appendix A.1, including MoETuner and Expert Race as the closest discussed work. Additional references support the new vision, adversarial, leakage, and SFT material. This substantially changes the research lineage and novelty argument.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, research question, and substantial methodology and experimental passages are rewritten. Experiments are reorganized into language and vision sections; earlier ablations, detailed language results, and the Jacobian discussion move into a reorganized appendix. Limitations and ethics also move to the document's end.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one. The opening MTEB heatmap is replaced by vision routing examples, the mechanism diagram is redrawn, and new capability, vision, corruption, radar, and learning-curve displays are introduced. Earlier tables and router visualizations are extensively relocated and resized.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful scoring analyses and tests robustness and cross-domain applicability beyond v1's clean language experiments. However, the retained Jacobian proof is not adapted to the new sigmoid score, and Figure 8 retains classification values that disagree with the revised MTEB tables. New vision attack strengths are also unspecified. These support and reporting gaps affect central additions, preventing a reliable judgment that the expanded evidence produces a net quality improvement.
